title: Measuring the impact of AI on software engineering  – with Laura Tacho
summary: DX CTO Laura Tacho pushes back on AI hype with measurement data: headline code-share figures are misleading, gains depend on enablement, small batches and stability.

assertions.quote: those headlines suggest that 30% of Microsoft's code that's running in production was authored by AI. That is not at all realistic.

verdicts.note: Google and Microsoft executives cite ~25-50% of new code AI-generated; the figures are self-reported and usually count accepted suggestions, not finished code.

assertions.quote: Do we really want to measure AI impact in terms of lines of code generated? I certainly don't. We don't recommend it.

verdicts.note: Accepted suggestions are often later rewritten or deleted, and output volume has long been a poor proxy for productivity; controlled studies measure task time or delivery instead.

assertions.quote: organizationally how fast we can create code has never been the bottleneck. It's been everything around it.

verdicts.note: Studies of developer time show coding is a minority of work; DORA and Faros 2025 found individual coding gains often don't translate into delivery throughput.

assertions.quote: stack trace analysis and refactoring existing code we're saving more time than the midloop code generation

verdicts.note: This comes from self-reported vendor survey data, which is known to misestimate time savings, though diagnosis tasks avoid the review overhead of generated code.

Developers praised AI for finding bugs and quick troubleshooting, but in the experiment debugging-style use lowered task output while raising accuracy. Reports of value exist, but no time saving was observed.

assertions.quote: many developers were actually feeling less satisfied because AI is accelerating the parts that they enjoy.

verdicts.note: DORA reported this pattern in one year's data, but other surveys find AI users report higher satisfaction, so the effect is mixed.

Anthropic: some engineers miss hands-on coding and find prompting unfulfilling, but people mostly delegate boring tasks (44% of Claude work was tasks they wouldn't enjoy), which is the opposite of the claimed mechanism.

assertions.quote: if AI adoption increases by 25% they actually predict that it's going to be a minus 7.2% 2% reduction in delivery stability

verdicts.note: DORA 2024 estimated a 25% AI-adoption increase associated with ~1.5% lower throughput and ~7.2% lower stability; DORA 2025 found throughput improved but instability persisted.

assertions.quote: Bigger batch sizes are riskier. >> So we want to keep batch size small.

verdicts.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.

assertions.quote: leaders re recommitting to like clean interfaces between services. I would say that's probably the top thing that comes up

verdicts.note: Clear module boundaries help both humans and agents navigate and test; consistent with Ousterhout and practitioner reports.

assertions.quote: for AI, it's really good to have the coding examples. There need can't be visual dependencies.

verdicts.note: Agents parse markdown and commands far more reliably than GUI instructions; llms.txt and markdown docs are spreading for this reason.

assertions.quote: they've had to be so intentional with acceptable use policies, with licensing ... And the more intentional and structured a roll out it is

verdicts.note: These come from DORA's 2025 AI capabilities model, a survey-based correlational analysis; plausible and consistent with older DORA findings on small batches, but not causal evidence.

assertions.quote: They really do need support and enablement and training

verdicts.note: Adoption and gains vary widely across teams and DORA finds organizational practices matter, but evidence isolating training effects is mostly observational.

assertions.quote: combining self-reported metrics with system and workflow metrics is absolutely essential when measuring the impact of AI tools

verdicts.note: Self-reports alone overstate speedups (METR) and telemetry alone misses experience and quality, so triangulating against a baseline is standard measurement practice.

assertions.quote: that's a really common pattern right now is using AI for migration

verdicts.note: Migration case studies (Google, Amazon Java upgrades, Airbnb) got their scale from pairing LLMs with deterministic tooling and validation rather than free-form generation.

assertions.quote: think about it more as experiment portfolios

verdicts.note: This is a strategic framing about how to organize product work rather than a measurable claim.
